zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical checkpoint: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510; supplied page subset consulted after independent scan reading. The scan remains authoritative. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

runs.text: A que não ouuera de dizer.

lines.note: Rǒ completes the preceding page's Nettô mǒxitçu-, the regretful wish not to have said something. This is body continuation, unlike the duplicate catchword at the foot of f361.
Nevobiye means waking in fright. The principal forms uru and eta agree with the following example; the Portuguese supplies both surprise and fear.
Com medo completes the fearful awakening. Nevobiyetaru begins the example, and teqi- continues into domo on the next physical line.
The frightened enemies are startled by the battle cry and become flustered. Toqino coye is the cry of battle; the line's printed Japanese spacing is retained.
Futamequ completes the paired description of agitation. The source label Taif. is followed by Lib. 8., whose clear two-loop numeral corrects OCR S; the Portuguese translation begins here.

runs.text: pertos com medo, & eſpantados com a voz, &

lines.note: The enemies awaken afraid and are startled by the soldiers' voices. This continues the Portuguese translation of the example above, not a separate sense.

Grita corrects OCR grira and denotes the soldiers' shouting. Reuoluerãoſe has no supported tilde over u. The abraded final mark after pertur is retained as a stop from the aligned OCR; a division mark is possible, but continuation alone cannot establish a hyphen.

Barãoſe finishes the preceding account of panic. At the far right, the printed parenthesis and eſpanto. complete the following Nevodoroqi gloss by backward overflow; they are preserved on this physical row, not joined to barãoſe or moved below the next headword.
Nevodoroqi is waking from sleep in alarm. Its Portuguese gloss ends with the displaced eſpanto. printed at the right of the preceding row, which the corrected placement explicitly preserves.
Nevoqi is the act or routine of going to bed and rising. The paragraph sign introduces an example whose Ne- continues into voqini on the next line.

Nevoqini Oraciouo mǒſu is saying a prayer when going to bed and rising. Oracio is incorporated into the Japanese example; its initial O is upright with the rest of the word, not an isolated italic. The scan's comma after deitarſe replaces the OCR stop.
The prayer is also said on getting out of bed. This completes the translation of the preceding Japanese example rather than adding another headword.

This verb concerns rising from sleep. The locally c-shaped vowel in Nevcqi is retained from the baseline although the neighboring noun and meaning suggest neoki; the damaged type is not silently regularized to Nevoqi.
The alternative Portuguese paraphrase is simply waking. It completes the preceding verb's gloss, while the next entry is separately marked for regional usage.
Nevozomi is another verb for awakening. The circumflex in ôda is distinct from a caron; the final X. is an upright usage label, here including its stop.
Neya denotes a sleeping chamber. Cubiculo de dormir describes the room, not the act of sleeping.

runs.text: Porta do cubiculo em queſe dorme.

lines.note: Neyanoto is the door of the sleeping chamber. The printed closed queſe is preserved rather than introducing modern word spacing.
Neyaxi denotes softening something. The scan supports the printed Amoſſar, not a normalization to Amaſſar; mol- continues into le on the following row.

runs.text: le, & brando como grude, maſſa, &c. Com-

lines.note: The objects softened include glue and dough. Com- begins the explanation of how commonly this verb is used in compounds.
Mummente completes Commummente. The compound example begins with Socuiuo, naming the rice paste described in the following translation.
Voxi neyaſu describes working or kneading the rice paste. The Portuguese gives Amaſſar and embaſteçer; the visible cedilla is retained rather than substituting modern spelling.

runs.text: certo grude feito de arroz cozido.

lines.note: The substance is a particular glue made from cooked rice. The scan supports grude, correcting OCR grade and agreeing with the preceding example's Socui.
Nezame is waking from sleep, here used with ſuru. The printed terminal hyphen is retained before the next line's object particle uo.

The second example describes an elderly person's waking and leaving part of the night unslept. The printed-looking separation nez amede and damaged yono are retained. An object-particle expression youo would fit the sense, but this does not establish the damaged letters.

runs.text: Deixar parte da noite ſem dormir, eſper

lines.note: Coſu completes the Japanese verb begun no- above. The Portuguese says to leave part of the night without sleeping; eſper continues below without an invented terminal hyphen.

The main text completes the explanation of waking because of old age. The separate far-right parenthesis and ſono. belong to the following Nezamegachi definition by backward overflow; this previously omitted word is restored at its physical location.
Nezamegachi denotes frequently waking from sleep. Its missing-looking final word is actually the displaced ſono. on the preceding row, not a new line below this entry.

runs.text: Vinho que ſe bebe antes de dormir.

lines.note: Nezaqe is wine drunk before sleeping, a bedtime drink. The Portuguese vinho names the beverage without specifying a modern category.
Nezumi is glossed simply as rato. This short independent entry supplies the animal name used in the following compounds.

runs.text: Poſtigo que ſe deixa ſò aberto pera

lines.note: Nezumido is a small wicket or opening left available for people to enter. The gloss continues with its use at a theatre or similar setting; the grave in ſò is retained.
The small entrance admits people into a theatre or a comparable enclosure. This completes Nezumido rather than referring to a literal passage for rats.

runs.text: Ratoeira, ou laçõ de tomar ratos.

lines.note: Nezumitori is a rat trap or snare. The scan restores u in the headword and the final stop after ratos; the abraded laçõ is retained without normalizing its mark.
Nezumivana gives another name for the same trap. Idem refers back to Nezumitori, and X. is an upright regional label rather than part of the italic gloss.
Nezumochi is a tree name. The dictionary supplies only that it is a tree so called; a botanical identification is not inserted into the transcription.

runs.text: O Fazer certo ſom com aboca ar-

lines.note: Nezunaqi denotes making a particular mouth sound. The gloss keeps its printed capital Fazer and closed aboca; ar- begins the imitation explained below.

runs.text: remedando o chiar do rato como pera fazer

lines.note: The sound imitates a rat's squeak and is made to prompt an animal's behavior. This continues the single definition, not another example sentence.

runs.text: choutar, ou dar couces o caualo, ou pera cha-

lines.note: The imitation can make a horse move at a particular gait or kick, or serve as a call. The line-ending cha- is visibly continued by mar below.
The call can attract a dog or cat. Nezunaqiuo ſuru exemplifies doing or making this squeaking sound, with the object particle attached as printed.

runs.text: Cugumelo que nace ao pee das

lines.note: Nezutaqe is a mushroom growing at the foot of trees. The historical forms Cugumelo and nace are retained rather than modernized.

runs.text: aruores à ſemelhança de pee de rato.

lines.note: The mushroom is compared to a rat's foot. The scan has continuous ſemelhança and doubled ee in pee, correcting the OCR's internal space and omitted e.
Nezzu is the saliva of someone asleep. The example begins with Nezzu- and continues with the attached object particle on the next row.
Nezzuuo taruru exemplifies drooling in sleep. Babarſe dormindo is the Portuguese translation; the divided word is not rejoined across physical rows.
Nezzumi is pinching. The clearly marked principal form ûda replaces OCR ſida, and the initial B of Beliſcar replaces E; Cami introduces the regional equivalent on the next line.
Tçumeru is the Cami equivalent of the preceding pinching verb. Its visible capital T replaces OCR r, and the word remains italic as part of the Portuguese regional explanation.

The new N-before-H section begins with a two-line enlarged N followed by upright Hacudǒ. The synonym Vacaxuno michi concerns relations involving young men; the historical source glosses it as Sodomia. The missing initial and its physical extent are restored without modernizing the entry.

The source adds its condemnatory phrase peccado mao, with no extra i as in OCR. A Japanese example begins Nhacudǒuo tatçu- and continues at the top of column 2; the second physical row sits beside the enlarged N.

runs.text: Ser paciente neſte abuſo, ou peccado

lines.note: Ru completes tatçuru from the foot of column 1. Ser paciente describes taking the receptive role in the behavior named by the preceding entry, using the source's own historical terminology.
Mao completes the source's phrase peccado mao. Como por officio adds the sense of doing this as a regular occupation; the evaluative language belongs to the dictionary.
Nhacuſô is explained by Vacaiſô, a young Buddhist monk. The Portuguese begins Bonzo, ou Religioſo and supplies the age qualification below.
Mancebo completes the definition: the monk is young. The short continuation belongs to Nhacuſô, not to the following entry for woman.
Nho is equated with Vonna and glossed Molher. The historical Japanese v and Portuguese spelling are retained.
Nhôbǒ refers back through Idem to the preceding woman entry. The two vowel marks are different: circumflex on the first o and caron on the second.
Nhôbǒgurui concerns sexual involvement with women, which the source glosses as fornication. The final i is visible, and Fornicação restores the printed a in place of OCR e.
The example uses the preceding noun with uo ſuru. The scan restores the initial Nh rather than OCR Nn and retains the same marked vowels as the headword.
Nhobon is paraphrased by Vonnauo vocaſu. The Portuguese describes sexual wrongdoing involving a woman; initial Nh is supported by the tall second-letter stroke, not OCR Nn.
Molher completes the preceding Portuguese gloss. It is a continuation line, not another Japanese headword or an independent Portuguese entry.
Nhôfachi and Nhôfat are alternative names for paired metal percussion instruments. The label l, introduces the alternative rather than another gloss.

runs.text: bronzo, ou metal que à maneira de ſeſtros fa-

lines.note: The instruments are of bronze or another metal and are compared to ſeſtros. The historical bronzo and the printed comparison are retained without replacing them with a modern instrument name.

runs.text: zem ſoar tocando hum no outro. ¶

lines.note: They sound by striking one against the other. The paragraph sign introduces an example, with Nhô- physically divided from fatuo below.
Nhôfatuo naraſu means making these instruments sound. The Portuguese repeats ſeſtros; the baseline estes is retained without a speculative long-s substitution.
Nhofô is gentleness or mildness. Its circumflex is on the second o; this spelling is preserved rather than made to resemble neighboring Nhô- heads.
Nhofôna, optionally followed by fito, describes a gentle person. The Portuguese Homem manſo confirms the adjectival use.

runs.text: Dignidade da molher do Dairi antes

lines.note: Nhôgo names the rank of a woman associated with the Dairi. Dairi is a Japanese title embedded within Portuguese prose, not an independent synonym.
The rank is described as preceding the status the dictionary calls Rainha. This completes the preceding court-title definition without expanding it into a modern historical classification.
Nhogui is equated with Vonna and glossed as woman. The i, is a linking label; Vonna remains part of the Japanese explanation.
Nhoi is illustrated by Nhoi manzocu. Couſa, visibly ending in a rather than OCR e, introduces something done or accomplished in accordance with a person's wishes.

runs.text: prida à võtade dalguẽ, ou cõtẽtamẽto perfeito.

lines.note: The gloss is accomplishment to someone's wishes or perfect contentment. Enlargement shows three abbreviation marks in cõtẽtamẽto, including the previously missed one on the final e; no missing n is silently expanded.

runs.text: O fazerſe a Rainha, ou outra peßoa de

lines.note: Nhôin concerns a woman of the highest court rank, or another noble person, entering religious life. The detailed process and adopted name continue below.

runs.text: caſta de Cũgues, freira, ou raparſe, tomando

lines.note: The person comes from the Cũgues and becomes a nun or has the head shaved. Cũgues is a Japanese court-social term embedded in Portuguese, with its printed tilde retained.
The adopted name ends in In. The scan shows the entire Japanese name element upright, correcting the OCR's split l/n typography; the preceding comma is retained.

runs.text: Facilidade em menear a lingua pera

lines.note: Nhôjet denotes facility in moving the tongue for speech. Initial N and the descending j are visible, correcting OCR Rhôiet; the following adjectival entry repeats the same root.

runs.text: pronunciar quaes quer palauras, & falar expe-

lines.note: This facility allows pronunciation of any words and fluent speaking. The historical separation quaes quer and the line-ending expe- are retained.
Ditamente completes expeditamente, describing fluent or ready speech. The short continuation belongs to Nhôjet, not to the next adjective.
Nhôjetna, also used before fito, describes a person with this verbal facility. The abbreviations q̃ and tẽ are preserved without expansion.
Esta facilidade na lingua completes the adjective's explanation by referring back to the preceding entry. It adds no new headword or example.

runs.text: Vagar em fazer as couſas com per-

lines.note: Nhônet denotes taking time to do things with perfection. The scan separates com from per and shows a raised terminal division mark; per- continues into feição below.
Feição completes perfeição, the care or perfection sought in doing things slowly. The physical division is retained rather than reconstructed as a single-line word.
Nhônetna describes something done slowly and perfectly. The scan restores the circumflex in the headword and the f of perfecta-, whose cross-stroke distinguishes it from the OCR long s.
Mente completes perfectamente. Nhônetna fito then applies the same quality to a person, whose behavior is explained on the next row.

runs.text: faz as couſas de vagar, & com exacção.

lines.note: The person does things slowly and with exactness. The historical separation de vagar and spelling exacção are preserved.
Nhônetni is the adverbial form, linked to Netçǔ. Adu. is the Portuguese grammatical label; the gloss begins by saying slowly or deliberately.
Perfeitamente completes the paired adverbial gloss. The line belongs to Nhônetni, not to the next woman entry.
Nhonin is glossed as woman. Its plain vowels are retained independently of the accented forms in neighboring entries.
Nhorai is a name or designation of Fotoque. Fotoque occurs inside the Portuguese explanation and is recorded for optional whole-word font review.
Nhoraifada denotes a certain mild, perceptible warmth. The gloss's ſenſiuel means capable of being felt, not a modern English psychological sense of sensitive.

runs.text: que ſe ſente em algũa couſa.

lines.note: The warmth is felt in some object or substance. The tilde in algũa is retained on u, without shifting it to the adjacent a.
Nhôran denotes disorder or confusion, explained by Midare. The scan supports Nh rather than OCR Nin; this is a flush-left independent entry, and the terminal S. is an upright written-usage label.
Nhotai is paraphrased as Vonnano tai, a woman's form or body. The historical Portuguese ſustancia is retained rather than regularized to modern substância.
De molher completes the preceding definition of a woman's form. Its indentation is that of a continuation, unlike the independent heads below it.
Nhoxi is glossed as daughter. The scan places it at the normal headword margin, so the provisional continuation indent is removed.
Nhôxi denotes the spur or projecting beak of a ship. Its circumflex distinguishes it from the preceding daughter entry, and it begins at the normal headword margin.
Nhoxǒ is equated with Nhonin and glossed as woman. The caron is retained, and the independent headword's false continuation indent is removed.

runs.text: Nhǔbu. i, Fajimete chiguiǒ nadoye yuqu.

lines.note: Nhǔbu denotes first going to one's fief or a similar place. The damaged u retains a faint second stroke and caron; NINJAL independently identifies Nhǔbu. The worn internal i and marked o in chiguiǒ are chosen from their remaining traces and the Japanese context, not interpreted as a sentence-breaking dot. Both damaged readings remain nonblocking caveats.

zones.label: Column 2 catchword
zones.note: Isolated bottom-right Tomar is a catchword, not an additional body row; the following page is outside this package.
